How Hospital Money Is Organized: Operating and Capital Budgets, Cost Centers, the Fiscal Year

Unit 1: Financial Management. Lesson 1 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

A budget packet lands on your desk with a return date three weeks out. It has two sections you must fill in, it is addressed to a number rather than to your department's name, and it asks for next year rather than this one. Before you can fill in a single line you have to know which pot of money each request belongs in, whose signature releases it, and which twelve months you are being asked about.

Operating money and capital money are different money

The operating budget is the coming year's running expenses, plus any revenue the department earns. Labor, parts, service contracts, outside labor, calibration, small tools, supplies, travel, memberships, and education all live here. An operating dollar is spent and gone inside the year.

The capital budget is for items with a long useful life whose price clears the hospital's capitalization threshold: a monitoring system, a large analyzer, a shop expansion, major test equipment. A capital item is not charged against this year at full price. It is recorded as an asset and depreciated across its useful life, so your operating budget feels only the depreciation and the service that follows it. Capital requests compete against every other capital request in the hospital, which is why they need the clinical case attached.

Who approves what

Request                      Approved by                                  Why
Operating budget             your own chain of command plus finance       it is this year's spending
Capital request              the capital or technology committee and      capital money is rationed
                             senior leadership                            across the whole hospital
A purchase inside budget     the manager, up to a policy dollar limit     the money is already approved
A purchase over the limit    the next level and purchasing                a second signature on size
An unbudgeted repair         finance, by exception, in writing            it has to come from somewhere

The fiscal year and the cycle

The hospital's fiscal year is its twelve-month accounting year, and it often does not start in January. Know which year a request is aimed at before you write it. Budgets are typically built three to six months before the fiscal year starts, and the cycle repeats: request, review and negotiation, approval, then monthly reports against the approved plan for the rest of the year.

Cost centers and where HTM money comes from

A cost center is the numbered account a department's costs post to, and the HTM department is one of them. Every work order, part, and contract payment should trace to a cost center, because that is the only way cost can be allocated back to the department that owns the device. Your funding arrives three ways: the department's own budget, the service contracts the department manages on other departments' behalf, and chargebacks that bill a clinical cost center for parts or labor spent on its equipment.

Distributed versus consolidated budgeting

Under distributed budgeting HTM holds only shop costs, and contracts, parts, and outside labor stay with whichever clinical cost center owns the device. Nobody can then see the total cost of maintaining a device, and nobody with the vendor's invoice in hand has the technical standing to hold that vendor to its terms. Under consolidated budgeting every equipment dollar moves under the HTM cost center and is allocated back to the clinical cost centers from CMMS reports. That is the stronger model, because the department that pays the invoice can withhold payment until the service report arrives. Consolidation only holds together with a written fiscal agreement among HTM, the clinical departments, and the chief financial officer on priorities and on how a repair that exceeds the budget still gets done.

Exam tip: expense this year means operating; long-lived and above the threshold means capital. Operating goes up your chain with finance, capital goes to the capital committee. Consolidated budgeting gives the manager control and visibility; distributed budgeting takes both away.
Remember
Operating money is this year's expenses and capital money buys long-lived assets that get depreciated, each approved by a different body, all of it posted to a cost center inside a fiscal year that may not be the calendar year.
Deeper explanation

How Hospital Money Is Organized: Operating and Capital Budgets, Cost Centers, the Fiscal Year, explained slowly

Walking one dollar through the hospital

The fastest way to understand hospital money is to follow four requests that arrive in the same week and watch where each one goes.

Request                              Pot        Approver                    Timing
A $280 pressure transducer for the   operating  the manager, inside the     today
shop's test bench                               policy limit
A $4,100 vital signs monitor to      capital    the capital committee, if   next fiscal
replace a failed unit                            it clears the threshold     year
A $38,000 unplanned repair on an     operating  finance, by exception, in   this month
imaging system out of contract                   writing
A $1,900 training seat for a         operating  the manager plus whoever    this quarter
technician                                       controls education money

Three of the four are operating money and one is capital, and the only reason the monitor is capital is that it clears the hospital's capitalization threshold and has a long useful life. Change the threshold and the same device becomes an operating purchase. That is why the first question on any request is never "how much" but "which pot".

The cycle, month by month

A fiscal year that starts in October is built in April and May, reviewed and negotiated in June, approved in July or August, and reported against from November onward. Work backward from that and two habits follow. First, the data you will use to build the budget has to exist by March, which means the cost history, the contract list with renewal dates, and the replacement plan are maintained all year rather than assembled in a panic. Second, a device you want in October has to be in the capital list written eighteen months earlier, so the clinical conversation starts long before the clinical department feels the need.

Consolidation is not a bookkeeping preference. It is the difference between a manager who can prove a contract is overpriced and a manager who can only suspect it.

The irregular cost trap

A device needs a $14,000 assembly every eighteen months. Budget from last year's actual spending and the line is zero, because last year's cycle fell outside the year. Two years later the cost arrives twice in one year and the variance report looks like mismanagement. Large costs that recur on a long interval must be budgeted on their interval, not on last year's actual, and the chief financial officer decides how such a cost is carried: spread across years, held in a reserve, or taken as an exception when it lands. Ask the question before the fiscal year starts, in writing, and the answer protects you twice.

What to memorize

Operating budget      this year's expenses and revenue, spent and gone
Capital budget        long-lived items above the capitalization threshold,

Fiscal year           the hospital's twelve-month accounting year; often not
                      the calendar year
